Field surveys of the Black-ribbed mussel (Septifer virgatus) have documented its early life history in considerable detail. Newly metamorphosed juveniles, immediately following settlement and the loss of the velar apparatus, possess a prodissoconch shell length of approximately 0.039 centimeters [Lb = approximately 0.039 centimeters], a value that reflects the size at which the post-larval individual begins its benthic existence. This initial shell dimension is minute, even by bivalve standards, indicating that the species undergoes a substantial planktotrophic larval phase before attaining metamorphic competence. In laboratory rearing trials conducted at a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the embryonic period from gamete fusion to the hatching of the first free-swimming veliger was observed to be quite brief; veliger larvae emerged from the egg capsule just 1 day [ab = 1 day] after fertilization. This rapid developmental onset is likely an adaptation to maximize the duration of the planktonic feeding stage in warm, productive coastal waters. The relatively tiny larval size at hatching imposes a high dependence on exogenous phytoplankton resources from the earliest moments of the veliger phase.

As the veliger larvae grow and develop through the pediveliger stage, they eventually attain a shell length that marks the onset of reproductive maturity. For Septifer virgatus, the length at which puberty occurs has been estimated from gonadal inspection of field-collected individuals to be 1.5 centimeters [Lp = 1.5 centimeters], a threshold at which gametogenesis is first detected in the developing gonad. At this size, the corresponding wet weight of the animal in somatic and reproductive tissues is approximately 0.1 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.1 grams], indicating a relatively lean body composition at the transition to adulthood. Reaching this critical size requires a considerable investment of time under natural thermal regimes. When maintained at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the time since birth required for an individual to reach this pubertal stage has been measured at approximately 365 days [tp = approximately 365 days]. This extended juvenile phase, lasting roughly one full year under warm conditions, suggests that the species prioritizes somatic growth and shell accretion before diverting resources toward reproductive functions.

The maximum or ultimate total length achieved by Septifer virgatus in dense intertidal populations has been recorded at 6.5 centimeters [Li = 6.5 centimeters], a dimension that represents the asymptotic size of the largest adults found within favorable habitats. At this final size, the corresponding ultimate wet weight of the soft tissues, excluding the shell, reaches 5.81 grams [Wwi = 5.81 grams], reflecting the substantial mass of the mantle, gills, and adductor muscles required for filter-feeding and attachment. The relationship between shell length and tissue mass in this species appears to follow a typical allometric trajectory for mytilid bivalves, with a disproportionate increase in tissue weight relative to shell length as the organism approaches its maximal dimensions. These maximum values are most commonly observed in older individuals that have experienced minimal disturbance from wave action or predation and that inhabit the mid-intertidal zone where food availability is consistently high. The attainment of such a size likely confers a reproductive advantage, as larger individuals can produce a greater number of gametes during each spawning cycle.

Reproductive output in the Black-ribbed mussel is substantial, and estimates of the maximum daily reproductive rate have been derived from comparative data within the Mytilidae. At a maintained water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], reproductive activity is most intensive, and the species spawns approximately 1,000,000 oocytes per event [N_R_i = approximately 1,000,000 oocytes per event] during the peak of the spawning season. When considering the continuous nature of spawning in warm-water populations, this translates to roughly 1 spawning event per day [F_R_i = roughly 1 spawning event per day], for an annual output of approximately 1,000,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 1,000,000 eggs per year]. This daily spawning frequency places Septifer virgatus among the most fecund of the mytilids, comparable to the high output seen in the Pacific oyster Crassostrea gigas, from which the initial estimate of gamete production was extrapolated. The energetic cost of such a sustained reproductive effort is considerable, likely requiring the mussel to maintain high filtration rates to secure sufficient organic particulates from the surrounding water column to fuel both somatic maintenance and gametogenesis simultaneously.

Longevity data for Septifer virgatus indicate that individuals can attain a maximum lifespan of approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years] when maintained under laboratory conditions at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] with ad libitum food supply. This considerable lifespan, which spans more than 4,380 days, is notable for a relatively small intertidal bivalve, as many congeners in temperate regions typically survive for only three to six years. The slow accumulation of somatic tissue over the first year of life, represented by the long juvenile phase of approximately 365 days [tp = approximately 365 days] until maturity at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], appears to be a life-history strategy that prioritizes the construction of a durable, thick shell capable of resisting wave dislodgement and drilling predation. Senescence in this species is gradual, with the oldest individuals exhibiting reduced filtration rates and a marked decline in the condition index of the adductor muscle. The trade-off between a prolonged reproductive window and the energetic demands of late-life maintenance is stark, as the largest, oldest females continue to spawn until shortly before death.
